newsitem.title: FRANCE: French cabinet prepares key policy statement.
newsitem.headline: French cabinet prepares key policy statement.

text.p: France's new Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin met his cabinet on Thursday to prepare a first statement to parliament on how to turn election promises into jobs.

Before the two-hour working session, Jospin met European Commission President Jacques Santer and said afterwards that France's concern to redirect European economic policy towards promoting growth and jobs had been "understood".

Less than two weeks after the left won power, Jospin faces intense pressure from France's partners to agree to the European Union's budget stability pact, a condition for the planned single European currency, at a summit in Amsterdam next week.

He is also under conflicting pressures at home from unions calling for wage hikes and pushing him to keep campaign promises to create 700,000 jobs for young people and cut the working week to 35 hours from 39 with no cut in pay.

Aides said Jospin would outline his policies in his first statement to parliament on June 19 and announce key dates for implementing his programme -- a revised budget and a national conference on jobs, wages and working hours bringing together government, employers and trade unions.

The policy statement in the National Assembly is traditionally followed by a confidence vote. The newly-elected 577-member assembly was due to meet for the first time later in the day, with Socialist ex-prime minister Laurent Fabius set to be elected speaker.
Unlike the regular weekly cabinet meetings chaired by President Jacques Chirac at his Elysee palace, the ministers met at Jospin's Matignon office across the Seine river.

The working session ended with the first official picture of the cabinet, without Chirac, who has refused to pose with the ministers at the Elysee -- a symptom of the uneasy "cohabitation" or power-sharing between the conservative president and a left-wing government.
In a test of cohabitation, the government sent for Chirac's signature a decree removing the head of the Paris criminal police, Olivier Foll.

The previous, conservative government had kept Foll in his job in an open challenge to courts which had suspended his investigative capacities. The suspension followed Foll's order to his men last year to refuse to help an investigating magistrate search the home of Paris mayor Jean Tiberi, a Chirac protege, in a sleaze probe.
Official sources said Interior Minister Jean-Pierre Chevenement wanted Foll, 58, to be replaced by Patrick Riou, 50, currently spokesman of the national police headquarters.
Chevenement also said he plans to propose new changes in France's tough immigration laws, last revised earlier this year when the centre-right controlled parliament.

"My goal is to draft a bill for the autumn session," he told reporters. A Socialist manifesto issued during last month's parliamentary election campaign had pledged to repeal the earlier legislation, drafted by Chevenement's hard-line predecessor, Gaullist Jean-Louis Debre.
Chevenement denied there were disagreements in the cabinet over reports from official sources that tens of thousands of illegal immigrants could be granted residence permits.
"There is not the shadow of a cigarette paper between the prime minister and myself," he said.

The conservative daily Le Figaro said Chevenement was furious over the effect of the announcement as opinion polls show a majority of voters oppose repealing hardline laws passed by the conservatives to curb illegal immigration.
